RespIrometry trials conducted under controlled thermal conditions revealed that the basal oxygen consumption of Neotamias alpinus reaches a maximum of 57.87 milliliters per hour [JOi = 57.87 milliliters per hour] at a stable core temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This elevated metabolic rate, measured in post-absorptive adults during the inactive phase of their daily cycle, is relatively high compared to other sciurids of similar body size and likely reflects the energetic demands of a montane existence where thermoregulatory costs are substantial even during rest. The measurement was obtained from a captive individual acclimated to laboratory conditions, ensuring that the value represents a true basal state rather than a field metabolic rate influenced by activity or digestion. Such data are crucial for understanding the energetic landscape of this alpine specialist.

Reproductive output in this species is characterized by a modest annual rate, with females producing a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year]. Within that single annual event, a female typically gives birth to a litter of 4 to 5 pups [N_R_i = a litter of 4 to 5 pups]. This combination of a single litter per year and a moderate litter size reflects a slow life-history strategy typical of many small mammals inhabiting harsh, high-elevation environments where the window for successful rearing is short. The interval between successive litters, spanning an entire year, means that a female can only produce one cohort of offspring annually, limiting the species' capacity for rapid population growth even under favorable conditions. This reproductive schedule is likely constrained by the long period of maternal care required.

At a stable core body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], a comprehensive analysis of life-history data, drawing on comparisons with the closely related Neotamias panamintinus, indicates that the maximum lifespan for this species in the wild is approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years]. This longevity is notably extended for a mammal of its size, which typically averages around 45 grams [Wwi = around 45 grams] for adult females. The ultimate wet weight for females can range from 27 to 45 grams, but the upper end of this range, representing the heaviest individuals, is most commonly recorded in reproductively active, well-nourished adults preparing for winter hibernation. This substantial adult mass is supported by a relatively prolonged gestation period of 24 days [tg = 24 days], allowing for significant fetal development prior to parturition at a temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C].

The neonatal stage is brief, with newborn pups weighing approximately 5.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 5.8 grams] at birth, a value inferred from data on the closely related species Neotamias panamintinus. Under a core body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], weaning occurs at 21 days after birth [tx = 21 days after birth], marking the point at which the pups begin to consume solid food and achieve nutritional independence from the dam. This rapid weaning age is characteristic of small-bodied sciurids and allows the mother to regain body condition before the onset of winter. The swift transition from a milk-based diet to solid foods is critical for the juveniles to accumulate sufficient fat reserves for their first hibernation. Post-weaning, the young must grow rapidly.

Sexual maturation is a delayed process in this species, with puberty being attained at 365 days since birth [tp = 365 days since birth] under a core body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This means that individuals born in the summer of one year do not reach reproductive maturity until the following summer, effectively creating a two-year generation time from birth to first successful breeding. This extended pre-reproductive period is ecologically significant, as it means that population turnover is inherently slow, making the species vulnerable to prolonged periods of low recruitment following environmental perturbations. The physiological changes associated with this maturation, including the development of gonadal tissues and the onset of hormonal cycles, are tightly linked to seasonal cues and photoperiod in their high-altitude environment. This life-history trait underscores the conservative reproductive strategy of this alpine chipmunk.
